checklist_item.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Are peers penalized for sending over-cap transactions?
checklist_item.notes: Source: PROP-W3B12-19, Trust Boundaries: tb-002, tb-009. Peer flooding protection.

code_scope.resolution_error: Prysm is a consensus-layer client; individual transaction gas-limit cap enforcement is an execution-layer concern handled by execution clients (e.g., geth/reth). Prysm does not receive individual transactions via P2P and does not implement per-transaction gasLimit > 16777216 validation or peer scoring for this condition.

audit_items.state_context: Prysm's beacon-chain/sync package handles beacon block gossip and RPC, not transaction pool P2P. Transaction propagation is handled exclusively by the execution client layer. The Engine API boundary between Prysm and the execution client does not include per-transaction gas cap checks on Prysm's side.

phase1.name: Abstract Interpretation
phase1.summary: Searched Prysm for: (1) transaction gas limit enforcement, (2) peer penalty for over-cap transactions, (3) gasLimit > 16777216 validation. Found no relevant code. Prysm's P2P layer handles beacon objects (blocks, attestations, blobs), not execution-layer transactions. The 16777216 literal in Prysm relates only to HISTORICAL_ROOTS_LIMIT and INACTIVITY_PENALTY_QUOTIENT_BELLATRIX beacon chain constants, unrelated to transaction gas caps.
attack_vectors_considered: Could an attacker send crafted gossip messages to Prysm that trigger gas-limit-related processing? No — Prysm's gossip topics are beacon-layer only.
Does Prysm re-broadcast execution transactions? No — execution transaction propagation is delegated entirely to the attached execution client.

Could an attacker abuse the Engine API between Prysm and the EL to force Prysm to process over-cap transactions? No — Prysm only queries the EL via Engine API for block building/validation, not transaction pool management.
phase1.conclusion: Property is not applicable to Prysm. The trust boundary described (P2P transaction propagation with gas cap enforcement) belongs to the execution layer.

phase2.name: Symbolic Execution
phase2.summary: No code path exists in Prysm that accepts, validates, or scores peers for sending over-cap transactions. There is no symbolic path to trace because the functionality does not exist in this codebase.

phase2_5.name: Adversarial Challenge
phase2_5.summary: Adversarial question: Could there be a subtle interaction where Prysm's block validation indirectly enforces or fails to enforce transaction gas caps, leading to a vulnerability? Checked beacon-chain/sync/validate_beacon_blocks.go — Prysm validates block structure and consensus properties, delegating execution payload validity to the EL via engine_newPayload. This means EL-side gas cap enforcement is the responsibility of the execution client. No Prysm-side vulnerability identified.
phase2_5.guards_challenged: N/A — no guard exists in Prysm for this check

phase3.name: Invariant Proving
phase3.summary: Invariant: 'Prysm penalizes peers sending transactions with gasLimit > 16777216.' This invariant cannot hold because Prysm does not process execution-layer transactions via P2P. The property is architecturally inapplicable.
phase3.conclusion: Invariant is vacuously false for Prysm — the system does not perform this function.

phase3_5.name: Final Adversarial Review
phase3_5.summary: No vulnerability found in Prysm related to this check. The audit target (Prysm consensus client) is architecturally separated from execution-layer transaction handling. Any vulnerability in this domain would need to be assessed against the execution client (e.g., geth, reth, besu) in a separate audit.

audit_items.reasoning: CHK-0019 checks whether peers are penalized for sending transactions with gasLimit > 16777216. Prysm is a consensus-layer (CL) client that does NOT handle execution-layer (EL) transaction propagation. Individual transaction gas limit enforcement is exclusively an execution-layer concern. Prysm's P2P layer handles beacon protocol messages (blocks, attestations, blob sidecars), not EL transactions. No code in Prysm performs per-transaction gas cap validation or peer penalty for over-cap transactions. This check is architecturally out-of-scope for Prysm and should be evaluated against the paired execution client.

checklist_item.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Is ModExp multiplication_complexity >= 16 for all inputs?
checklist_item.notes: Source: PROP-W3B12-20, Trust Boundaries: tb-007, tb-008. Complexity floor prevents DoS.

code_scope.resolution_error: ModExp (EIP-198/EIP-2565) is an EVM execution-layer precompile. Prysm is a consensus client and does not implement EVM precompiles. No ModExp-related code exists in the Prysm codebase.

audit_items.state_context: Searched Prysm for: 'ModExp', 'modexp', 'mod_exp', 'MODEXP', 'precompile', 'EIP-198', 'bigModExp', 'multiplication_complexity', 'adjExpLen'. No matches found in the core codebase (only an unrelated fileutil.go match for 'modexp' as part of another word). Prysm does not execute EVM code.

phase1.name: Abstract Interpretation
phase1.summary: ModExp precompile gas computation (multiplication_complexity >= 16 floor) is a property of EIP-2565 (Big integer modular exponentiation gas cost). This EIP specifies how the EVM execution client prices calls to the 0x05 precompile address. Prysm, as a consensus client, never executes EVM transactions or precompiles. The EVM execution is delegated entirely to the attached execution client via the Engine API.
attack_vectors_considered: Could an attacker craft an execution payload that contains a ModExp call with underpriced gas and pass it through Prysm to the EL? Prysm forwards execution payloads to the EL via engine_newPayload but does NOT validate EVM execution semantics including precompile gas costs. The EL is responsible for validating and rejecting such payloads.

Could Prysm's Engine API integration have a bypass that allows underpriced ModExp calls to be included in blocks? No — Prysm trusts the EL to validate execution correctness. If the EL rejects a payload, Prysm marks the block as invalid.
phase1.conclusion: Property is not applicable to Prysm. ModExp gas computation is exclusively an EL function.

phase2.name: Symbolic Execution
phase2.summary: No code path in Prysm computes ModExp multiplication_complexity. The EVM precompile execution is entirely within the execution client domain. No symbolic path to trace.

phase2_5.name: Adversarial Challenge
phase2_5.summary: Adversarial question: Could there be a way that Prysm's gas validation for execution payloads (block-level GasUsed check) creates a vulnerability related to ModExp underpricing? Prysm validates block-level GasUsed <= GasLimit but does not validate the breakdown of gas consumption per EVM operation. An underpriced ModExp would affect the EL's gas accounting, not Prysm's. The EL would report the correct GasUsed after execution, which Prysm then validates against the declared GasLimit.
phase2_5.conclusion: No Prysm-side vulnerability. EL is the correct target for this check.

phase3.name: Invariant Proving
phase3.summary: Invariant: 'ModExp multiplication_complexity >= 16 for all inputs processed by Prysm.' This invariant is vacuously true for Prysm because Prysm never computes ModExp complexity. The EL is responsible for this invariant.

phase3_5.name: Final Adversarial Review
phase3_5.summary: Confirmed out of scope. This property (CHK-0020) must be audited against the paired execution client (e.g., go-ethereum, Nethermind, Besu, Reth) which implements the ModExp precompile.

audit_items.reasoning: CHK-0020 checks the ModExp precompile (EIP-2565) multiplication_complexity floor of 16. Prysm is a consensus-layer client that does not implement EVM precompiles. The ModExp precompile exists at address 0x05 in the EVM execution layer. Prysm does not execute EVM code; it delegates execution to the attached execution client via Engine API. Extensive search of the Prysm codebase found zero instances of ModExp, precompile gas computation, or adjExpLen. This check is architecturally out-of-scope for Prysm.

checklist_item.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Is complexity exactly 16 when max_length <= 32?
checklist_item.notes: Source: PROP-W3B12-21, Trust Boundary: tb-007. Boundary inconsistency causes consensus failure.

code_scope.resolution_error: ModExp complexity formula (complexity = 16 when max(base_length, modulus_length) <= 32) is an EVM execution-layer precompile calculation. Not present in Prysm.

audit_items.state_context: Same as CHK-0020: Prysm does not implement ModExp. No code handling the 'max_length <= 32' branch exists in the Prysm codebase.

phase1.name: Abstract Interpretation
phase1.summary: The branch boundary check (complexity = 16 for max(base_length, modulus_length) <= 32, complexity = ceil(max_length/8)^2 * 2 for > 32) is from EIP-2565's multiplication_complexity function. This boundary condition, if incorrect, would cause cross-client consensus failures. However, Prysm is a consensus client and does not implement this calculation. The risk of consensus failure from this boundary error would manifest in execution clients, not Prysm.
attack_vectors_considered: Could an incorrect ModExp gas computation in one client cause a consensus split that Prysm would fork-choice incorrectly? Yes, if one EL charges different gas for ModExp, two chains could diverge at the execution payload level. Prysm would follow whichever chain its EL considers valid. However, this is an EL-level issue, not a Prysm-level issue.
Could Prysm's fork-choice logic amplify an EL ModExp consensus split? Theoretically possible as a second-order effect, but this is not a Prysm-side vulnerability.
phase1.conclusion: Direct implementation check is out-of-scope for Prysm. Second-order consensus split risk exists but is owned by the execution layer.

phase2.name: Symbolic Execution
phase2.summary: No ModExp complexity calculation code path exists in Prysm. No path to trace.

phase2_5.name: Adversarial Challenge
phase2_5.summary: The 'Tampering' risk category suggests this check is about consensus correctness — if one client computes complexity = 16 where another computes complexity != 16, you get a gas cost divergence and a potential chain split. This is a valid concern for multi-client Ethereum. However, the Prysm consensus client is not the implementation layer where this divergence would occur. The risk is real but belongs in EL audit scope.
phase2_5.conclusion: Out of scope for Prysm as the CL implementation does not compute ModExp complexity.

phase3.name: Invariant Proving
phase3.summary: Invariant: 'For any ModExp call with max(base_length, mod_length) <= 32, Prysm computes complexity = 16.' Prysm never computes ModExp complexity; the invariant is vacuously inapplicable.

phase3_5.name: Final Adversarial Review
phase3_5.summary: The note 'boundary inconsistency causes consensus failure' is important context. If Prysm's EL integration allows execution payloads with incorrect gas accounting to propagate, there could be a second-order Prysm issue. However, Prysm validates execution payloads holistically via engine_newPayload — the EL either accepts or rejects. Prysm does not verify individual transaction gas computations. Out of scope.

audit_items.reasoning: CHK-0021 checks the ModExp complexity boundary condition (exactly 16 when max_length <= 32). This is an EIP-2565 EVM precompile property. Prysm does not implement EVM precompiles or ModExp gas computation. Although cross-client ModExp consensus divergence could have second-order effects on Prysm's fork-choice, the root cause and fix lies in execution client implementations. Out of scope for Prysm audit.

checklist_item.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Is complexity formula correct for max_length > 32 with overflow protection?
checklist_item.notes: Source: PROP-W3B12-22, Trust Boundary: tb-007. Overflow wraps gas cost enabling DoS.

code_scope.resolution_error: ModExp complexity overflow check (for max_length > 32, complexity = 2 * ceil(max_length/8)^2) is an execution-layer EVM precompile calculation. Not present in Prysm.

audit_items.state_context: Searched for: 'iteration_count', 'multiplication_complexity', 'adjExpLen', 'ModExp', 'bigModExp', 'words^2'. No matches in Prysm core code. This property is specific to EIP-2565 which operates in the EVM execution layer.

phase1.name: Abstract Interpretation
phase1.summary: The critical-severity integer overflow in ModExp complexity computation (words^2 for large inputs) is a gas underpricing vulnerability that could allow DoS against the network. If 'words' is computed as a uint64 or similar bounded type and words^2 overflows, the effective complexity becomes very small, allowing expensive computation at near-zero gas cost. This is a well-known class of bug. However, it resides entirely in the EVM execution layer. Prysm does not compute this value.
attack_vectors_considered: Direct overflow attack: Attacker sends a transaction with very large base_length/modulus_length to trigger overflow in words^2. This would affect only the execution client.

Prysm relay attack: Could Prysm be used to propagate blocks containing overflowed-gas ModExp transactions? Prysm forwards execution payloads as-is to the EL. If the EL's gas accounting is incorrect due to overflow, the EL would still accept the block (because it computes the same wrong gas cost). This doesn't create a distinct Prysm vulnerability.
Cross-client inconsistency: If one EL has the overflow bug and another does not, a chain split could form. Prysm would follow its EL's assessment.
phase1.conclusion: Critical finding for execution clients, but out-of-scope for Prysm consensus client.

phase2.name: Symbolic Execution
phase2.summary: No code path for ModExp complexity computation exists in Prysm. The words^2 overflow cannot occur in code that doesn't exist.
phase2.conclusion: No applicable code path in Prysm.

phase2_5.name: Adversarial Challenge
phase2_5.summary: This is a Critical severity item (overflow wraps gas cost enabling DoS). Adversarial question: Is there any way this affects Prysm specifically? Could a malformed execution payload with overflowed gas accounting cause Prysm to enter an inconsistent state? Answer: No. Prysm's validator sends the payload to engine_newPayload. The EL returns VALID or INVALID. Prysm acts on this response. If the EL incorrectly accepts an overflowed-gas transaction, Prysm accepts the block. This is an EL bug, not a Prysm bug.
phase2_5.conclusion: Confirmed out-of-scope for Prysm. Should be escalated to EL audit.

phase3.name: Invariant Proving
phase3.summary: Invariant: 'Prysm rejects execution payloads where ModExp gas overflows.' Prysm cannot enforce this invariant because it does not compute ModExp gas. The EL is the enforcer. Prysm trusts the EL's validity determination.

phase3_5.name: Final Adversarial Review
phase3_5.summary: This is a Critical finding that warrants separate execution-layer audit. For Prysm: the architectural trust boundary (Prysm trusts EL for execution validity) means this overflow cannot be detected or mitigated by Prysm. The EL pair must be audited separately. Out of scope for this Prysm audit.
phase3_5.conclusion: Out of scope for Prysm. IMPORTANT: This property should be re-queued for an execution client audit.

audit_items.reasoning: CHK-0022 checks for integer overflow in ModExp complexity computation (words^2 for max_length > 32 inputs). This is a Critical-severity EVM precompile vulnerability that would allow an attacker to perform expensive computation at artificially low gas cost (DoS). However, Prysm is a consensus client and does not implement the ModExp precompile or compute multiplication_complexity. This check is entirely out-of-scope for the Prysm codebase. It must be evaluated against the execution client (go-ethereum, Nethermind, Besu, Reth). Note: This property is important and should be re-triaged for execution client audit coverage.
recommendations: Re-triage CHK-0022 for execution client audit scope
Verify integer overflow protection in go-ethereum's precompile/big_mod_exp.go

checklist_item.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Is iteration_count exactly 1 when exponent is 0?
checklist_item.notes: Source: PROP-W3B12-23, Trust Boundary: tb-007. Zero exponent edge case.

code_scope.resolution_error: ModExp iteration_count (exponent bit-length handling) is an EVM execution-layer precompile calculation. Prysm does not implement this.

audit_items.state_context: Searched for 'iteration_count', 'adjusted_exp', 'adjExpLen', 'exponent.*count', 'exponent.*bit'. No relevant results in Prysm. This property is specific to EIP-2565 Section 4 (adjusted_exponent_length calculation for exponent = 0 edge case).

phase1.name: Abstract Interpretation
phase1.summary: The iteration_count (adjusted_exponent_length) = 1 when exponent = 0 is a specific edge case in EIP-2565's gas formula. Without this floor, exponent = 0 would yield iteration_count = 0, causing a division-by-zero or zero gas cost. This edge case is critical for correct gas pricing. However, it exists in the EVM execution layer, not in Prysm.
attack_vectors_considered: Zero exponent attack: Attacker sends ModExp with exponent=0, exponent_length<=32. If iteration_count is incorrectly 0, gas = max(500, complexity * 0) = 500 still applies due to the max(500,...) floor — but if the max() guard is also missing, gas = 0, enabling free computation.
Cross-client divergence: If one EL treats iteration_count=0 differently from another, gas costs diverge, causing chain splits.
Could Prysm be affected? No — Prysm does not compute iteration_count.
phase1.conclusion: Property is not applicable to Prysm. Zero exponent handling is an EL precompile concern.

phase2.name: Symbolic Execution
phase2.summary: No code path in Prysm computes adjusted_exponent_length or iteration_count for ModExp. The zero exponent edge case cannot be analyzed in Prysm because the code doesn't exist.

phase2_5.name: Adversarial Challenge
phase2_5.summary: The 'Tampering' risk category suggests this check is about consensus correctness. If iteration_count is wrong for exponent=0, two clients would compute different gas costs, potentially causing a chain split. This is important for Ethereum consensus safety but is implemented in execution clients. Adversarial question: Could Prysm's block proposal or validation logic be affected? No — Prysm uses the EL to execute transactions and trusts the reported GasUsed. The iteration_count error would only manifest within the EL's EVM interpreter.

phase3.name: Invariant Proving
phase3.summary: Invariant: 'For ModExp with exponent=0, Prysm computes iteration_count=1.' Prysm never computes iteration_count. The invariant is vacuously inapplicable to Prysm.

phase3_5.name: Final Adversarial Review
phase3_5.summary: CHK-0023 is a High-severity zero input handling check for ModExp iteration_count. Like CHK-0020/0021/0022, this belongs entirely in the execution client domain. Prysm does not implement EVM precompile logic. The consensus-split risk from incorrect iteration_count handling is real but must be addressed by execution client teams. Out of scope for Prysm.

audit_items.reasoning: CHK-0023 checks whether ModExp iteration_count is exactly 1 when exponent = 0 (to prevent zero-gas or division-by-zero scenarios per EIP-2565). This is an EVM precompile implementation detail in execution clients. Prysm is a consensus client that does not implement the ModExp precompile or compute adjusted_exponent_length. No relevant code exists in the Prysm codebase. This check must be evaluated against execution client implementations (go-ethereum, Nethermind, Besu, Reth).
recommendations: Re-triage CHK-0023 for execution client audit scope
Verify zero-exponent iteration_count handling in go-ethereum's core/vm/contracts.go
